agent_notes: Miktam is of uncertain meaning. Rashi gives three options (a musical term; from 'mach ve-tam', humble and whole; from 'ketem', gold), Ibn Ezra 'a precious psalm, like fine gold', Targum a 'engraved/chiselled' piece (גליפא תריצא). I transliterate and gloss it as 'a miktam' in the literal layer and keep the debate in the commentary. The title is verse 1 of the Hebrew; the KJV counts it as 16:0.

agent_notes: Rashi on 'תודיעני': 'future tense, not a prayer'. Radak reads it as a prayer. Hebrew imperfect can be either; I translated 'you will make known' (as the word table does) and drew out the future sense in the dramatic layer. 'נעימות' is a plural 'pleasant things'; the KJV 'pleasures' is more sensual than the Hebrew, which is about sweetness and delight. 'נצח' is 'perpetuity/duration', not necessarily 'eternity' in the later sense.

agent_notes: Revised after review. The verb אָמַרְתְּ is feminine singular, so the speaker is addressing a 'you' who is feminine. The commentators split: Rashi first has David speaking to the congregation of Israel, then, as an alternative, to his own soul (compared with 'vattekhal David', 2 Sam 13:39 as Rashi cites it); Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take the soul; Malbim takes the feminine 'you' as the nation that worships other gods; the Targum has 'my soul'. The five English versions: KJV, ASV, BBE and Webster add 'O my soul', YLT does not. The last clause is the hard one (KJV 'my goodness extendeth not to thee', ASV/BBE 'no good beyond/but you'). I keep the literal 'my good [is] not upon you' and lay out the readings in the commentary.

agent_notes: Revised after review. Ibn Ezra is not in the 'patriarchs' camp: he says that explaining the holy ones as the patriarchs does not fit the sense of the psalm, and that 'in the land' is needed because 'holy ones' usually means angels. Rashi (the buried righteous) and Meiri (the patriarchs, dead and in the earth) read it of the dead; Radak and Metzudat David of living pious people to learn from; Malbim of idols. The syntax is open: 'to the holy ones' may be a dative of benefit ('for the sake of'), an address, or a heading for the last clause. My literal keeps the Hebrew's fragmentary shape.

agent_notes: 'אחר מהרו' is split: (a) 'who hurry after another [god]' (KJV, BBE; Rashi, Radak's first reading, Ibn Ezra), (b) 'who pay a bride-price/purchase another' from mohar, Gen 34:12 and Ex 22:15 (ASV 'give gifts'; Radak, Metzudat Zion, Meiri's second reading), (c) YLT 'hastened backward'. My literal layer has 'hurried [after] another', the commentary explains the mohar option. 'מדם' I render 'from blood', which could mean 'of blood' (made of blood), 'with blood' or 'from [shed] blood'; Radak reads it as ill-gotten and as a prophetic comparison (Mal 1:13) rather than literal. Radak's text is partly missing and I did not rely on it beyond what it states.

agent_notes: 'תומיך' is a puzzling form: Rashi (citing Sifrei) takes it from 'to bring low' (Eccl 10:18), Ibn Ezra and Radak compare it to the hiphil-like form of 'tamakh' (to hold, uphold), and Ibn Ezra rejects the comparison to mosia' as far-fetched. I gloss 'you are holding/upholding' and mention the alternative. 'וכוסי' as 'portion' (Ibn Ezra: from 'takhossu', Ex 12:4) vs 'cup of wine' (the usual reading, and the Ps 23:5 'my cup runs over' image).

agent_notes: 'נחלת' is the Hebrew's written form; Radak notes that the final taw stands for a hey (nachalah) as in 'ozi vezimrat Yah' (Ex 15:2), and that it is not a construct. I translate 'an inheritance' without 'of'. 'Strong's chevel' means a measuring cord, hence an allotted portion; both the line and the plot it marks are intended.

agent_notes: 'כליותי' is the kidneys, in Hebrew the seat of the inmost conscience and desire. The KJV has 'reins' (an old word for kidneys, which readers no longer recognize). ASV 'heart' and BBE 'thoughts' soften it. I kept 'kidneys' literally, as the skill requires. Rashi brings an alternative midrashic reading (Abraham learning Torah on his own) which I note but do not adopt.

'שויתי' is rendered 'I have placed' (also 'I have set', 'I have likened'): the root is shawah, to set or to level. The Metzudat Zion link to 'mesawweh raglai' (Ps 18) is a gloss, not a citation of mine. The Targum uses 'for his Shekhinah dwells upon me', which I did not borrow.

agent_notes: 'כבודי' is 'my glory' or 'my liver (kaved)'. The Masoretic text has 'kevodi' and every medieval source in the packet reads it as the soul or the honour (Radak and Metzudat David: neshamah, 'the glory of the body'). Acts 2:26 follows the LXX 'my tongue'. I did not cite the LXX because it is not in the packet; this is background knowledge, and I leave it out of the commentary. 'לבטח' is 'to security', not 'in hope': the KJV 'rest in hope' goes through the Greek of Acts, not the Hebrew.
